name: Oakmoss

card.summary: Oakmoss is a lichen extract used as a mossy, woody base note and fixative in chypre and fougere fragrances, part of how people build a personal scent.
card.note: A recognised fragrance allergen; regulators restrict atranol and chloroatranol.

quick.overview:
Oakmoss is a lichen, Evernia prunastri, harvested in South-Central Europe and processed in Grasse into absolutes. Perfumers use it as a base note and fixative with a woody, sharp, slightly sweet scent.

It matters for appearance mainly through fragrance: it is a key ingredient of classic chypre and fougere perfumes, which are styles often worn as part of a grooming routine.
quick.how: Oakmoss is not applied on its own; it is a component of finished perfumes and colognes. Many scents have been reformulated with substitutes because of restrictions.
quick.risks: Oakmoss absolute is one of the more frequent fragrance sensitisers in patch-testing. Its allergens atranol and chloroatranol are prohibited in cosmetics in the EU under Regulation 2017/1410. People with known fragrance allergy are advised to avoid it.

lead: Oakmoss (Evernia prunastri) is a lichen that grows mainly on oaks but also on other trees in temperate Northern Hemisphere forests.[1] Its extracts act as fixatives and base notes in perfumery, and are key components of chypre and fougere fragrances.[1]

Dermatology reviews list oakmoss and treemoss absolutes among the frequent fragrance sensitisers.[2] The EU has prohibited atranol and chloroatranol, its main allergens, in cosmetics, and industry self-regulation limits their levels.[3][4]

chain: Lichen absolute is blended into a perfume base
Wearer carries a mossy, woody scent
angle.text: Oakmoss contributes to how a fragrance smells and lasts on the skin. It is part of a perfume that people wear for scent presentation rather than a treatment for the skin itself.

paras: The lichen is harvested in South-Central Europe and sent to Grasse, where absolutes are extracted; the scent is woody, sharp and slightly sweet.[1] Industry restrictions have led many fragrances to be reformulated with substitutes.[1]

A 2020 review notes that up to 4.5% of the general adult population may be allergic to fragrance materials, with oakmoss absolute among the most frequent sensitisers.[2] Atranol and chloroatranol are the main culprits, and a 2021 study of non-animal methods suggested that additional compounds in oakmoss may also sensitise skin.[4]
German surveillance data showed positive patch tests to fragrance mix I falling from 9.1% in 2012 to 4.6% in 2021, after the EU prohibited the allergens.[3]
No studies found on cosmetic benefit. Patch-test surveillance of fragrance allergy is described above, and laboratory and rat studies have examined oakmoss extracts for other properties.[5]

timeline.event: Linnaeus describes the species as Lichen prunastri.[1]
EU Regulation 2017/1410 prohibits atranol and chloroatranol in cosmetics.[3]
